stewart_read: The rep's opener names Ion and references Carol's request but the person answering still needs a second beat of clarification, suggesting the initial legitimacy framing landed thin for someone who wasn't expecting the call.
alternative_hypothesis: This could simply be a third party (not Carol) answering Carol's phone, which would explain the confusion regardless of intro quality.
coaching_implication: When a third party answers, a slightly fuller reference (company + reason + what Carol requested) before asking to speak with her may reduce this friction, though it is a minor point given the intro does self-correct at 00:06.

stewart_read: Rather than reflecting back what the rep already heard (a 'free solar' expectation) to keep control of the frame, the rep asks an open question that lets the customer restate and escalate her frustration before the rep responds.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have been buying a beat to hear the specific complaint before responding, which is reasonable given the customer's original line was unclear ('Yes. All I wondered is if if, our solar would be covered.').
coaching_implication: A brief reflect-back ('sounds like you were told it'd be free — let me clarify what our program actually covers') could shorten the runway to the scam comment that follows.

quote: Solar is just a scam, but I appreciate your call.
stewart_read: Customer explicitly frames the experience as a scam after the free-solar expectation wasn't met. No script-defined rebuttal in Ion's current schema maps cleanly to this marketing-expectation-gap version of the trust objection — the closest schema entry (how_did_you_get_my_number) addresses a different concern (how contact info was obtained), not this one.
coaching_implication: This is a known gap: Ion's rebuttal library does not yet have a canonical response for 'free solar in my ZIP code' expectation mismatches leading to scam framing. Worth flagging to Kenny as a rebuttal to add (schema section 10, currently TBD list already includes 'scammer_anecdote_reframe').

quote: We don't have free solar. We have a no upfront, no out of pocket cost solar, but it's not free. You'd still have to pay for the equipment.
stewart_read: This is not actually a knowledge gap in the negative sense — the rep gives an accurate, honest correction of the marketing claim rather than fabricating a 'free solar' story to keep the call alive. This protects trust even though it doesn't recover the sale.
alternative_hypothesis: A less disciplined rep might have leaned into the free-solar framing to keep the customer engaged; the rep chose accuracy over a short-term save.
coaching_implication: Reinforce this as a good habit in the 1-on-1 — correcting inflated marketing promises directly, without over-explaining or panicking, is the right instinct even on a call that ultimately DQs.

quote: Well, do you already have solar, Carol?
stewart_read: Once the customer signals 'we're good' about coverage, the rep correctly pivots into the orphaned-flow qualifier rather than continuing to argue the free-solar premise — this is the schema-correct move for a customer who may already own a system.
coaching_implication: No coaching needed here; this is the procedural right answer and should be named as such rather than treated as an avoidance of the scam comment.

quote: And do we use Solar Energy World, Frank? We use Solar Energy World.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers the name of her existing installer unprompted — free competitive intel — but the rep does not follow up on it (e.g., system size, satisfaction, when installed) before closing the call.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the customer had just stated clear disinterest, spending more time probing could have felt like pushing on a closed door; the rep may have judged disengaging as the better read.
coaching_implication: Even on a call ending in DQ, a 10-second probe ('how's that system working out for you?') costs nothing and can surface useful context or even a future re-engagement angle.

quote: Okay? Okay. No problem. Have a good one.
stewart_read: The call ends abruptly with no acknowledgment of the earlier scam comment and no attempt to leave the door open (e.g., for the state-incentive angle she asked about). This is a DQ call, so a full button-up isn't expected, but the exit is purely reactive with no closing frame.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the hard DQ (existing system + explicit disinterest), a minimal exit is defensible — there is no appointment to protect and continued engagement risks irritating a customer who has already declined twice.
coaching_implication: Not a high-priority fix given the DQ status, but a one-line acknowledgment of her original concern ('makes sense you'd want to know if it's covered — glad we could clarify') would leave a slightly better final impression at negligible cost.
